degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: Regenerated cellulose is biologically attacked, but visible loss of textile fibers and conversion to carbon dioxide are different endpoints.

recyclingAndEndOfLife:
Mechanical textile recycling opens and shreds fibers for reuse, but the resulting shorter fibers may need stronger carrier fibers for spinning. Lenzing’s 2025 report describes commercial REFIBRA recycling of cotton or regenerated-cellulose textile waste, blended with virgin pulp to produce new fibers; its ECOVERO viscose example contains at least 20% recycled material. This is a defined manufacturer route rather than a guarantee that every blended garment is accepted.

A laboratory Ioncell study directly redissolved white, black and blue Danufil viscose and white Lenzing modal in the ionic liquid [DBNH][OAc], then regenerated lyocell-type fibers by dry-jet wet spinning. The fibers were made into yarn and knitted demonstrators. This demonstrates reuse of these low-degree-of-polymerization regenerated fibers; mixed textile waste and dye removal remained further development work.

recyclingAndEndOfLife:
Established paper recycling reclaims cellulose-rich fibers by repulping sheets in water, screening and cleaning contaminants, and forming new paper. For coated fine papers, Sappi describes flotation deinking, further washing and bleaching, and blending recovered fibers with virgin fiber and mill broke. Fiber damage and contamination affect the resulting paper quality; repulping recovers fibers rather than purified glucose monomer.

Cellulosic textiles also enter dissolution-and-regeneration routes. Lenzing reports commercial REFIBRA use of pre- and post-consumer cotton or regenerated-cellulose textile waste together with virgin pulp to make new fibers. Mechanical textile shredding is another route, although fiber shortening can require blending with carrier fibers before spinning. These paper and textile processes apply to selected cellulose-rich waste streams; they do not establish equivalent recyclability for every coated or composite cellulose article.

degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: Acid hydrolysis removes acyl side groups from poly(2-oxazoline)s, producing polyethyleneimine-containing chains and the corresponding carboxylic-acid products. Deacylation is not cleavage of the entire carbon–nitrogen backbone.

Timescales: The reported controlled reactions use strong aqueous acid and temperature-dependent reaction periods. No family-wide environmental mineralization time follows.

Environmental persistence: Side-chain chemistry strongly affects hydrolysis, and persistence of the residual PEI-containing polymer is a separate question.
recyclingAndEndOfLife: Controlled hydrolysis and subsequent functionalization provide laboratory routes to reuse polymer backbones as new functional materials. The paper does not demonstrate a post-consumer collection or closed-loop monomer-recovery system.

degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: Hypochlorite aging of PVP-containing membranes generated succinimide functionality and carboxyl-containing products associated with opening of pyrrolidone rings, and could remove PVP from the membrane.

Timescales: Accelerated chemical-cleaning exposure is not an environmental half-life. No condition-qualified natural mineralization time is provided.

Environmental persistence: Leaching of water-soluble PVP or its fragments transfers material to water; it does not by itself establish biodegradation.

degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: Poloxamer 407 can suffer sterilization-induced molecular changes; degradation must be distinguished from reversible gel dissolution on cooling or dilution. The source does not establish a complete degradation-product inventory.

Timescales: The cited work examines defined sterilization treatments and subsequent functional properties; no environmental half-life is assigned.

Environmental persistence: Disappearance of a poloxamer gel does not show mineralization of its PEO and PPO blocks. Environmental fate depends on block size and formulation.

degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: In a deliberately crosslinked PAMAM microgel, remaining amines cleave ester-containing links by aminolysis, releasing smaller dendrimer-containing species. This does not show destruction of ordinary PAMAM dendrimers.

Timescales: The modified microgels were followed for up to 72 hours in pH 5.3 or 7.4 buffer at 37 °C; behavior was pH dependent.

Environmental persistence: Network breakup and formation of nanoscale fragments are not mineralization. No environmental lifetime is established for the dendrimer family.

degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: Si–O bond cleavage can yield silanols, including dimethylsilanediol; this downstream product undergoes microbial conversion to carbon dioxide in the studied soils. Catalyzed recycling instead generates cyclic siloxanes such as D4–D6.

Timescales: The soil study measures dimethylsilanediol fate, not the overall PDMS lifetime. Rapid solvent/catalyst depolymerization is not an ambient-degradation timescale.

Environmental persistence: Polymer formulation, crosslinking, soil contact and cleavage to mobile silanols must be distinguished. Biodegradation of isolated dimethylsilanediol does not establish rapid disappearance of an intact silicone article.
recyclingAndEndOfLife: Acid/base-catalyzed depolymerization and recovery of cyclics are chemical-recycling routes. A public patent demonstrates fluoride-catalyzed depolymerization in swelling solvents, quenching and repolymerizable cyclic recovery at laboratory scale; it also addresses separating silicone from mixed objects.

degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: Air oxidation introduces hydroxyl and carbonyl groups into polyacetylene and destroys electrical conductivity. Oxygen uptake can increase specimen mass despite chemical degradation.

Timescales: The NBS report observed chemical change in films oxidized at 50 °C for 40 hours and continued oxidation during months at room temperature. These are oxidation and conductivity endpoints, not mineralization.

Environmental persistence: Loss of conjugation or conductivity does not prove the carbon has been biologically mineralized; soil and aquatic lifetimes remain an evidence gap.

degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: Oxidative degradation of PANI electrodes produces quinone-containing species, including p-benzoquinone; chain cleavage and hydrolysis differ from reversible doping/dedoping.

Timescales: The cited work follows chemical and electrochemical changes during cycling in aqueous zinc-sulfate electrolyte. Cycle stability is not a calendar time for environmental mineralization.

Environmental persistence: Electrolyte composition and operating potential affect electrode degradation; these results do not quantify persistence in soil or natural water.

Degradation products and pathways: Overoxidation introduces hydroxy and carbonyl groups into PPy. Removal of chloride dopant by alkali is a separate dedoping process and does not demonstrate destruction of the backbone.

degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: P3HT photooxidation produces carbonyl-containing structures and oxidized sulfur intermediates; side-chain cleavage and loss of conjugation accompany the changes. Specific sulfur-species assignments include uncertainty.

Timescales: Controlled thin-film experiments vary light spectrum/intensity, oxygen, humidity and temperature; there is no single transferable calendar lifetime.

Environmental persistence: The approximately 100 nm film studies measure chemical/optical aging, not complete mineralization of bulk P3HT in soil or water.

degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: Strong oxidant exposure can irreversibly shorten conjugation or chains in PEDOT; sulfur oxidation and ring opening are proposed mechanisms. Reversible gas-induced doping must be distinguished from this irreversible damage.

Timescales: The cited chemiresistor study uses repeated five-minute nitrogen-dioxide exposures with recovery intervals. Electrical resistance change is not a mineralization timescale.

Environmental persistence: Device-aging experiments do not establish the lifetime or biological fate of dispersed PEDOT in natural waters or soil.

degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: In the studied PCL composite, solvent separation leaves PEDOT:PSS coatings recoverable on microspheres. This demonstrates physical reclamation, not chemical mineralization of either polymer component.

Timescales: No complete degradation time for PEDOT:PSS was measured in the recycling experiment.

Environmental persistence: A degradable surrounding matrix does not by itself establish biodegradation of the retained conductive coating; soil and aquatic persistence remain unquantified.
recyclingAndEndOfLife: Selective PCL dissolution in ethyl acetate recovered intact PEDOT:PSS-coated microspheres. Thermal reshaping was also demonstrated for the composite. These are laboratory composite-recycling routes, not back-to-monomer recovery of PEDOT or PSS.

degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: Illumination alters MEH-PPV conjugation and creates optically distinct products. The cited fluorescence study resolves reactant decay and product buildup but does not establish a complete molecular product inventory.

Timescales: Kinetics were measured in o-dichlorobenzene in a cuvette and capillary optical fiber; the local illumination profile strongly affected the apparent rate. No environmental half-life follows.

Environmental persistence: Fluorescence loss in a photochemical experiment is not mineralization and cannot predict persistence of a solid film, device or environmental particle.

degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: In the representative poly(9,9-dioctylfluorene) studied here, thermal oxidation produces carbonyl-containing defects and changes blue emission toward green. A proposed radical mechanism includes fluorenone-type defects, alkyl ketones and crosslinking; it is not a complete product inventory for every polyfluorene.

Timescales: Pristine and solvent-aggregated films were aged in an oven at 60 or 90 °C for 1–72 hours. Optical and spectroscopic changes were measured; these accelerated tests do not establish an environmental degradation time.

Environmental persistence: Loss of useful luminescence does not demonstrate disappearance of the polymer backbone or biological mineralization. Substitution pattern, morphology and device construction prevent a family-wide lifetime assignment.
